Strength is graded and stable per surface form: highest (0.6-1.0 of the 2.40 scan max) on ' control'/' Control'/' controls'/' controlled'/' contro'/' uncontrolled' (1.7-2.2), ' effective'/' effectively'/' effectiveness'/' efficient'/' efficiently' (1.2-2.0), ' regulate'/' regulation'/' regulations'/' regulatory' (0.7-2.0), ' succeed'/' succeeded'/' successful'/' successfully'/'successor' (0.9-2.4), ' improve'/'improved'/'improving'/'improvement' (0.6-1.0), ' approved'/' authorized'/' audit'/' audits'/' comply' (0.8-1.2), ' eliminate'/'eliminated'/'erad'/'minimize'/' minimizing'/'maximize'/'optimized'/'optimal' (0.9-1.5), ' compete'/'competition'/'competitive'/'profit'/'profits'/'profitable'/'cooperate' (0.9-1.5), the calendar-date numeral tokens ' 1990'/'2000'/' 2000'/'1998'/' 1998'/'1999'/' 1996'/' 1988'/' 1980'-' 2004'/' Dec'/' December'/' Oct' (0.8-2.1, but ' 2018' reads 0.00 and ' 2010' 0.34), and the capitalised abbreviations or word-initial fragments of that register ('Comp'/' Comp'/' comp', 'Rec'/' rec', 'Reg', 'Impro', 'Micro', 'Motor', 'Machine', 'Robot', 'FDA', 'EC', 'NC'). A weaker band (0.25-0.6 of max) covers the rest of the management/technical vocabulary (' facilitate', ' implement'/'implemented'/'Implementation', ' establishing'/'establishment', ' coordinated'/'coordinating'/'coordination', ' modify'/'modified', ' utilized', ' refined', ' funded', ' promote', ' enhanced', ' influence'/'influenced', ' sustainable'/'sustainability', ' criminal'/'criminals', ' illegal'/'illegally', ' convict', ' ethical', ' Conservation', ' Forestry', ' wastewater', ' molecular', ' metabolic', ' amino', ' synthetic'), while it reads ~0 (below 0.1 of max) on ordinary vocabulary and on these semantically close non-members: ' support', ' health', ' safety', ' public', ' power', ' authority', ' management', ' development', ' integration', ' system'/'systems', ' program'/'programs', ' service'/'services', ' effects', ' drugs', ' companies', ' Congress', ' Senate', ' government', ' medical', ' water', ' food', ' children', ' cost'/'costs', ' investment', ' work'. Because member forms such as ' succeeded' (the scan maximum), ' cooperate', ' uncontrolled', ' minimizing', ' Fisheries', ' Implementation' and ' comply' occur too rarely to enter the scan's count>=3 top-token list, the claim is the word families and their documented strengths, not the top-200 token ids.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
For most of the twentieth century the weather station on the headland was run by two families who took turns keeping the log. The building itself was raised in stages: first a stone hut with a coal stove, then a wooden tower for the anemometer, and finally a brick annex where the instruments were stored and repaired. Visitors today see the annex as the oldest part of the site, though the records show it was the last to be built.

The log books are the reason the site still matters. Every four hours a keeper wrote down the wind direction, the height of the swell, the cloud cover, and any damage to the roof or the fence. The handwriting changes slowly across the volumes, and in some years two hands alternate, which suggests that a child or a spouse was filling in during an illness. Historians have used these entries to date storms that appear in no newspaper, and to check the accounts of ships that claimed to have passed the headland in fair weather.

Restoring the volumes took three winters. A conservator in the county archive first separated the pages that had stuck together after a leak in the ceiling, then brushed off the mould with a soft brush and a vacuum fitted with a filter. Each page was photographed twice, once under ordinary light and once with a raking lamp that made the indentation of the pen visible. The images were then stored on two drives, one kept in the building and one sent to a sister archive inland, because the headland floods in winter and the cellar has never been dry.

The trust that now runs the site wanted a full account of what had been spent before it applied for a second grant, so it commissioned an audit of the restoration accounts in the spring. The auditor found that most of the money had gone on labour rather than materials, and that the invoices from the photographic studio had been entered twice in one quarter. The trust accepted the finding, repaid the difference, and added a note to its annual report explaining what had changed.

Since then the station has drawn a modest but steady number of visitors, mostly walkers following the coastal path and school groups who come to see the instruments. The volunteers who staff the shop say the questions they hear most often are about the families who kept the log, and whether anyone still lives on the headland. Nobody does, but the anemometer still turns, and a copy of the readings is posted each month on a board beside the gate for anyone who wants to compare this year's weather with the weather of a hundred years ago.

The path itself is another matter. Two winters of heavy rain have taken away a stretch of the cliff edge south of the gate, and the council has closed that section while it decides whether to move the trail inland or build a retaining wall below it. The volunteers would prefer the wall, because the inland route cuts through a field where the ground nesting birds return each spring, but the wall is expensive and the council has said that any work will have to wait for a survey of the whole coastline. Until then visitors are asked to use the road, which adds half a mile to the walk and passes the old coastguard cottages, one of which now sells tea on weekends.
